name: Degema
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 8 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Kari, Ethelbert E. 2002. Distinguishing between clitics and words in Degema, Nigeria. African Study Monographs 23(4): 177-192. (publisher PDF via Kyoto University repository KURENAI, hdl 2433/68218)
catalog_locator: p.184, sec. 'II. An Accentual Test' (incl. ex. 23 and the sentence after it); NOTES (1), p.190.
catalog_quote: II. An Accentual Test Lack of independent accent has often been associated with clitics, whereas full words are considered as bearing accent. Degema clitics have no independent tone, i.e. underlying tone, unlike full words such as nouns, verbs, etc. However, they bear tone in the phonological word, since no syllable is toneless in such a word. Consider example (23): ... In the example above, the subject clitic that is toneless in (23a) bears a tone in (23b) as the verb forms a complex with it in the surface structure. ... NOTES (1) Degema has two tones — high and low, plus a downstepped high. In this paper, only the high tone and the downstepped high are marked.
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

new_statements.rule_in_words: Degema is described as a two-tone (H, L) language with downstepped H; 'accent' is operationalised as lexical tone (full words have underlying tone, clitics/affixes do not). None of the accessible descriptions says anything about word stress or its position.
new_statements.exceptions: none (tone: verbs lack lexical tone contrast per Rolle & Kari 2022 p.2; clitics/affixes toneless per Kari 2002a,b)
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical tone of words and tone assignment within the phonological word/phrase; no stress domain discussed. Corroborated by Rolle & Kari 2022 (lingbuzz/006614) p.2: 'Previous work has established two tones in Degema, high (H) and low (L), as well as surface downstepped high (ꜜH).' which never mentions stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All Kari sources and Rolle & Kari 2022 describe the Usokun (Usokun-Degema) variety; the other dialect is Atala/Degema Town. Both fall under dege1246 (no separate Glottolog dialect codes known to me).

tone_statements.citation: Rolle, Nicholas. 2026. Tone diachrony beyond tonogenesis: Reconstructing the tone melodies of nouns in Proto-Edoid (Niger-Congo). Ms. v3 (May 2026; v1 December 2025), lingbuzz/009572, 65 pp. Forthcoming in Diachronica. [PDF title page reads 'Tone diachrony beyond tonogenesis: Reconstructing the tone melodies of Proto-Edoid (Niger-Congo)', author affiliation Princeton University]
tone_statements.quote: Based on these intermediate reconstructions, we reconstruct tone in Proto-Edoid as a symmetrical set of melodies **L-L, **L-LH, **L-H, **L-HL, **H-L, **H-LH, **H-HL, and **H-H. From these Proto-Edoid melodies, we track several recurring tone changes, the most common of which are Rightward H-Shift (e.g. the Great Edo Tone Shift, *H-L > L-H), H-Obligatoriness (i.e. adding a H to all-L words), and H-Lowering (i.e. *H > ꜜH, M, or L).

tone_statements.quote: Degema orthography marks high tone with an acute accent ˊ and downstepped high with a macron ˉ ; low tone is not marked. ... In Degema, nouns are lexically contrastive for tone, but tone on verbs is determined solely by its grammatical context and not lexically specified. When verbs appear between a proclitic and an aspectual enclitic, all syllables are marked with high tone (H) ... Sentential negation is realized tonally by a high-low (HL) pattern: a high tone falls on the proclitic, followed by low tone on the verb.
tone_statements.summary: H, L and downstepped H; nouns lexically tonal, verb tone grammatical (H pattern; negation marked by an HL tone pattern alone); no tone count given; 'full tonology not worked out'; nothing on stress.

sources.quote: Previous work has established two tones in Degema, high (H) and low (L), as well as surface downstepped high (ꜜH). Tone is lexically contrastive on nouns, adverbs, ideophones, and grammatical items (but not for verbs). [...] In isolation, nouns are subject to two basic tone rules which alter their underlying forms: downstep is inserted between two final H's (e.g. /H-H/ → [HꜜH]), and H is inserted at the end of an all-low sequence (e.g. /L-L/ → [LH]). The combined effect of these rules is that virtually all nouns and noun phrases have a pitch change.
sources.locator: printed p. 1 (§1 Introduction, first quoted sentences) and p. 1 abstract; constraints (6) H-obligatoriness / Downstep-insertion / 3H-ban on printed p. 15 (§2.5…
sources.note: Degema nouns carry lexical tone in three main patterns (L-L, H-H, L-HH), with downstep inserted between two final highs and a final high added to all-low nouns in isolation. The paper also catalogs the tonal effects in 33 noun-phrase modification contexts and explains them by recursive phonological phrases and words; the catalog's lexical-tone class stands, and this adds the tone patterns, downstep and phrasal tone rules.
